summary: This memo specifies an Encapsulating Security Payload based mechanism for sending user data packets with the Host Identity Protocol. It obsoletes RFC 5202.

eli5.summary: Once two computers have agreed on secrets with HIP, this RFC says how to put data in sealed envelopes using ESP.

questions: how does hip rekey an esp security association
what is beet mode in ipsec
subtitle: How two hosts that have authenticated with HIP turn their shared secret into ESP-protected data traffic.

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol base exchange authenticates two hosts and produces shared keying material, but it defines no way to protect the actual user data that follows.
tldr.mechanism: The base exchange carries two extra parameters, ESP_TRANSFORM and ESP_INFO, so the hosts agree on a cipher suite and on SPI values, then create a pair of ESP Security Associations keyed from the shared material. UPDATE messages later replace those associations.
tldr.outcome: User data travels as ordinary-looking ESP packets, with the SPI standing in for the host identity. This RFC obsoletes RFC 5202.

today: RFC 7402 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 5202. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why HIP Needs a Data Format
sections.content:
In the Host Identity Protocol (HIP), hosts are identified by public keys. The HIP base exchange, defined in RFC 7401, lets two HIP hosts authenticate each other and create a HIP association. Along the way they generate shared keying material with an authenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange.

The base exchange does not describe a transport format for user data. It only says that implementing an Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) based format, as defined in RFC 4303, is mandatory. RFC 7402 fills that gap: it specifies a set of HIP extensions that create a pair of ESP Security Associations (SAs) during the base exchange, with keys drawn from the keying material, and methods to update those SAs later.

Middlebox traversal is out of scope. The RFC notes that HIP and ESP traffic have known issues with middleboxes and that other specifications cover running them over UDP.
sections.eli5: Showing your ID at the door is not the same as protecting what you say inside. HIP checks IDs; this RFC says how to protect the conversation afterwards.

sections.title: ESP Packets Carrying Host Identities
sections.content:
The HIP ESP packet looks exactly like an IPsec ESP transport format packet. What differs is the meaning. Host Identity is not carried in the headers of user data packets. Instead, the ESP Security Parameter Index (SPI) points to the right host context, so no extra protocol header is needed. The RFC calls the SPI a compressed representation of a pair of Host Identity Tags (HITs).

Each host chooses the SPI it wants to see on packets it receives, so it can pick different SPIs for different peers. The choice SHOULD be random, a different SPI SHOULD be used for each HIP exchange with a given host to avoid a replay attack, and the SPI MUST change when a host rekeys. Only the pair of destination IP address and SPI identifies the receiver at a given moment.

There are two ways to build this. An unmodified IPsec implementation can be used with extra upper-layer checksum processing that swaps IP addresses and HITs. Alternatively, BEET (Bound End-to-End Tunnel) mode formats the packet as transport mode but treats it as tunnel mode, with IP addresses as the outer addresses and HITs as the inner ones. BEET mode is internal to a host, so the peer does not need to implement it.

This use of ESP is for host-to-host traffic only. Security gateways are not supported.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing your full name on every envelope, you and your friend agree on a short code number. The number tells your friend which of your secret keys to use.

sections.title: Setting Up ESP in the Base Exchange
sections.content:
The ESP Security Associations are set up using parameters in the last three messages of the four-message base exchange: R1, I2 and R2.

  • In R1, the Responder lists the ESP transforms it is willing to use in an ESP_TRANSFORM parameter, in order of preference.
  • In I2, the Initiator picks exactly one of them and returns it in ESP_TRANSFORM. It also sends ESP_INFO holding the SPI it wants the peer to use when sending to it.
  • In R2, the Responder sends its own SPI in ESP_INFO, finishing the setup.

Each HIP association is linked to two ESP SAs, one for incoming and one for outgoing packets. The Initiator's incoming SA corresponds to the Responder's outgoing one, and the other way around. When a HIP association is removed, its ESP SAs MUST be removed too. All HIP packets, which use protocol 139, MUST bypass ESP processing.

If the Initiator supports none of the offered transforms, it should abandon the negotiation and tell the peer with a NOTIFY message. Two error values are defined for this: NO_ESP_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN (18) and INVALID_ESP_TRANSFORM_CHOSEN (19).
sections.eli5: One side shows a menu of ways to lock the envelopes. The other side picks one and says which code number it wants on its mail. Then the first side gives its own number back.

sections.title: The ESP_INFO and ESP_TRANSFORM Parameters
sections.content:
ESP_INFO (type 65, length 12) carries the SPI values and the KEYMAT index. Its fields are Reserved, KEYMAT Index, OLD SPI and NEW SPI. During initial setup, OLD SPI is zero because no earlier SPI exists, and NEW SPI is the SPI the sender wants the peer to use. The KEYMAT Index says, in bytes, where to continue drawing ESP keys from the keying material. It must be zero when an UPDATE carries a new Diffie-Hellman key. If the keying material runs out, the packet MUST contain a new Diffie-Hellman key.

ESP_TRANSFORM (type 4095) lists Suite IDs. A sender MUST NOT put more than six Suite IDs in one parameter, and a receiver MUST be ready to handle more than six. By default the parameter MUST contain at least one of the mandatory Suite IDs. In I2, it MUST hold a single value that matches one the Responder offered.

Both new parameters are covered by the HMAC and signature calculations in R1, I2, R2 and UPDATE packets.
sections.eli5: One form says "here is my old code number and my new one". The other is the menu of lock types, with at most six items on it.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
Every HIP implementation MUST support AES-128-CBC and AES-256-CBC. The mandatory suite for ESP_TRANSFORM is AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA-256 (Suite ID 8). NULL encryption with HMAC-SHA-256 (Suite ID 7) SHOULD also be supported, and NULL encryption MUST be used together with SHA-256 authentication.

An authentication-only suite, such as NULL, AES-CMAC-96 or AES-GMAC, MUST NOT be accepted if the peer offers it, unless local policy for that peer explicitly allows authentication-only mode. This prevents a session from being downgraded when one side wants privacy.

The Sequence Number field is MANDATORY and anti-replay protection MUST be used. A 64-bit sequence number MUST be used, so a host MUST rekey before its number reaches 2^64. The upper 32 bits are not in the ESP header and are kept locally by each peer.

HIP does not negotiate lifetimes. They are local policy. Implementations MUST support sequence number rollover as a lifetime and SHOULD support timing out inactive SAs.
sections.eli5: There is a short list of allowed locks, and one lock every computer must know. Computers also count their messages so an old message cannot be replayed, and they get a new lock before the counter runs out.

sections.title: Rekeying and Keying Material
sections.content:
Once both hosts are in the ESTABLISHED state there are no Initiator and Responder roles any more, and rekeying is symmetric. It uses the HIP UPDATE message. A host MUST rekey if its incoming ESP sequence counter is about to overflow, and may rekey at any time. It MAY include a new Diffie-Hellman key to generate fresh keying material. It MUST NOT replace its keying material until the exchange completes.

Each side must update its own half of the SA pair, including creating a new SPI, so each side both sends and receives an UPDATE. The old SAs stay in use for a while. A host starts sending on the new outgoing SA and may safely delete the old SAs once data arrives on the new incoming SA. A host MUST NOT generate new UPDATEs while it has an outstanding ESP SA update request, unless it is restarting the process, and it MUST NOT keep a request outstanding indefinitely.

ESP keys are drawn from the keying material after the HIP keys, in this order: encryption key then authentication key for the host with the greater HIT, then the same two for the host with the lower HIT. HITs are compared as unsigned 128-bit integers. During a rekey only the four ESP keys are drawn, not the HIP keys.
sections.eli5: Over time the locks wear out. The two computers swap in new ones without dropping the conversation: they keep using the old lock until the first mail comes in with the new one.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Coexisting with IPsec
sections.content:
The RFC says the security considerations of ESP itself are in the ESP specification. What is new here is initial keying material generation and updating of that material. The initial keys come from the HIP Diffie-Hellman procedure, and the setup messages are protected by the base exchange. UPDATE exchanges are protected with the HIP association keys, using both HMAC and signatures. The signing is done partly for the benefit of intermediate systems that need the new SPI values, which is why the contents cannot be encrypted.

When HIP runs next to a standard IPsec implementation, the SPI values used for HIP SAs MUST NOT be used for IPsec or other SAs, and the reverse. If an IPsec ESP SA in tunnel mode also applies, traffic MUST be encrypted with both the HIP ESP SA and the IPsec SA. In transport mode, local policy MAY skip the second encryption to avoid double encryption.

A host that gets an ESP packet with an unknown SPI MAY answer, subject to rate limiting, with an ICMP Parameter Problem pointing at the SPI field.
sections.eli5: Everything about agreeing on new locks is itself signed and checked. Mixing this system with another lock system is fine as long as the two never reuse the same code numbers.
